thread.title: Ten-Year Treasury Hits 3.11% - Kamikaze BOJ Policy Takes Aim At Trump Trade Policies

author: Daniel R Moore
title: Ten-Year Treasury Hits 3.11% - Kamikaze BOJ Policy Takes Aim At Trump Trade Policies
text:
One of the cardinal rules in investing is never leverage a depreciating asset, or one that has a high probability of depreciating in the near future, particularly in a rising interest rate environment. Going down this path in investing is akin to flying a suicide mission in a war. And now that US policy has shifted away from monetary accommodation as the primary economic juice to the Trump fiscal policy which has rocked the market with rising interest rates due to increased public financing requirements, stocks have become increasingly volatile, and begun to decline from the peak set in January 2018. And, sovereign wealth funds and International Central Bank Balance Sheets flush with dollar denominated assets priced relative to US interest rates are currently coming under pressure.
The driving force behind the pressure is US Treasury interest rates which are on a torrid pace higher. The US 10 Year over the past several days has pierced the 3.11% level for the first time since May of 2011, seven years ago to the day when the 10 year closed at a yield of 3.12% on its way downward to all-time lows in the 1.50% range in the summer of 2012 and again in 2016.
This chart pattern is indicative of a clear shift in trend, one where it is unlikely that the ultra-low depths charted 2 and 6 years ago will be re-visited. What is the driving force behind this trend reversal and why is the 10 Year rate accelerating higher so quickly? Not surprisingly, the force for change has a very clear impetus, the Trump economic policy which squarely puts in place a plan which as executed will unravel the past 30 years of trade and fiscal policy – if the new policy stays in place long enough. And the information that I will provide in this article clearly shows that the new path the US is on will continue to take interest rates higher, and the path appears to be at odds with the International Banking community wishes, in particular, the Bank of Japan. Investors who continue to play the tech bull market rally as this financial market reversal unfolds better be able to withstand a rough ride, because this market is a pawn in a high powered trade war chess game being played between Washington and countries, like Japan, China, Germany and Mexico, that have fed off of the US policy of persistent trade deficits for the past 25 years.
For the purpose of this article, I am going to focus on Japan in particular. And the reason I am doing so is because of a recent public interview comment made by BOJ Governor Kuroda in a CNBC interview in April 2018 regarding Japan’s debt level which is the highest among all major economies at 236% of GDP. The following comment by Kuroda was made in response to a question to a question about how Kuroda viewed the recent warning by the IMF about rising sovereign debt levels around the world, including the US.
Bank of Japan a Pivotal “Manipulator” in the US Stock and Bond Market Safe haven? I would say the BOJ balance sheet is Lehman Brothers and Bear Sterns to the power of 10 waiting to erupt on the world financial market.
BOJ Governor Kuroda in an interview with CNBC on April 23 rd , 2018 was careful to emphasize that from a world market perspective, his currency is viewed not as a risk, but a safe zone. He did so with a bit of disbelief himself.
He also emphasized that the BOJ “is by far the largest net foreign asset holder”. Sounds very much like a “too big to fail argument” – in other words, if the BOJ balance sheet crashes and burns, the world will feel our pain. Japan’s central bank policies are indeed playing an out-sized role in perpetuating inflated asset valuations in the US and keeping the world from entering a debt crisis - but is it really sustainable?
The BOJ balance sheet has expanded 4.47 times since May of 2009 to a whopping $5.3T. The BOJ balance sheet is bigger than that of the US Federal Reserve even though Japan’s economy is 1/4th the size of the US. Kuroda’s rational for why Japan’s asset buying program is beneficial to the world, not a source of risk, is that it is leveraged by debt completely held by Japanese residents and the BOJ (ha). The problem with this argument is that the assets held are not all valued in Japanese Yen, so there is a major currency risk mismatch. The assets owned by the BOJ are not just JGBs or even low risk US Treasuries; the BOJ asset holdings include stocks, particularly tech stocks and other fixed income assets throughout the world. And if you doubt the effect, both direct and in-direct, its warped policies have had on the US stock market, you need only take a look at the following data set since 1998:
Pay attention in particular to the reduction in the BOJ balance sheet leading up to the 2008 financial crisis, a negative correlation up to the point in time the financial system broke; and, the extremely high correlation in US stock values from the end of 2014 thru the end of 2017. Recall the US Federal Reserve stopped asset purchases in October of 2014 and is now in balance sheet reduction mode, also known as quantitative tightening or QT. Based on this data alone, I would say that any reversal of the BOJ policy is going to eventually have a serious negative impact on the value of risk assets and tech stocks in particular. There was a brief decline in the BOJ balance sheet in March 2018, and the downward momentum in stocks was visible in the trading pattern. The BOJ asset buying program resumed in April and US stocks recovered with tech stocks continuing to lead the rally.
International Trade Model is Broken Why is the BOJ allowed by the WTO to leverage its central bank balance sheet to manipulate US stock and bond prices? BOJ Governor Kuroda will say it is because Japan policy makers believe their currency would be overvalued if they did not take these out-sized measures. And, Kuroda said as much in the interview with CNBC.
I personally do not buy this explanation as the data are screaming that the oversized actions by the BOJ are intended for one purpose only, to maintain a trade advantage relative to the US. However, the data also show that when they withdraw asset buying measures for any length of time and the YEN appreciates as it did after Bush II applied pressure in his second term, and Reagan did so through in the Plaza Accord of 1986, the US stock market eventually tanked (1987, 2008). In other words, the BOJ position in the world financial market can have a vicious impact on US markets as the structure is heavily leveraged toward inflating US capital markets rather than their own domestic economy.
In my view, the whole sovereign government market manipulation game to gain trading advantage process is now reaching a major impasse. The Japanese economic model is founded on printing YEN for the purpose of buying US assets which in turn allows it to control the relative YEN / USD relationship. Initially Treasuries were the primary dollar asset purchased; however, the asset buying has expanded to stocks and other fixed income assets because Treasuries became limited when the Fed executed its QE program from 2010 to 2014. This process works as long as US trade policy continues to run large deficits and as Kuroda points out in his comment on April 23 rd to CNBC, “sustainability of the public finance is squarely – maintained”. He was talking about Japan’s public finance, but because it is so entangled with the US market, indirectly he was referencing the cooperative trade arrangement between Washington and Japan in which Japan provides the US capital to sustain its on-going consumption lifestyle while the US keeps its fiscal policy growth rate under control. In reviewing the comment, I believe he wanted to say “must be maintained”, but slipped and said “restored”, because he fully understands that the path President Trump has put the US on from a public finance standpoint is completely unsustainable if the Bank of Japan is going to continue to act as a kingpin in propping up the USD value of its massive balance sheet by continuing to print YEN.
For some investors, what I am saying here may be fully understood; others may be skeptical and continue to drink the “free trade” Kool-Aid because more trade cannot possibly be a source of a problem, only unwinding the process in place will create the problem, and no one wants that to happen so why believe that it will. But the reason that it will happen, regardless of how hard the BOJ or other International Banks may continue to lean in the opposite direction in the short-term to protect their trade position with the US, is that the entire last 25 years put the US in an “unsustainable” financial position. And the following series of charts make this point very visible as an $11T cumulative international trade deficit has been accumulated by the US in the last 25 years and interest rates fell to 0% rather than rising dramatically as would be expected in a real free trade world when an economy runs perpetual trade deficits:
I won’t bore you with the details and depth of research behind the entire interest rate cycle. You can draw your own conclusions about the cause and effects which have created the 75 year through to peak to trough cycle in US Treasury rates. But my opinions I share here are founded on a thorough review of both quantitative and qualitative data, and most are documented in my book, Theory of Financial Relativity . And what led to the rise of interest rates off the zero bound post WWII in the 1950s is precisely what Trump policy makers are trying to recreate in 2018 and beyond, a strong US economy with low unemployment and high real GDP. Government policy makers are not brilliant by nature; they use history as a guide to try to redirect the economy in hopes of sparking growth and prosperity. And the 1950s, after the feeble attempt by the Obama administration to try to make everyone believe we were reliving the “Great Depression”, are the next stop in the trip down memory lane for Washington policy makers.
The big impediment to the Trump plan is that the world is not presently in the 1950s, although we are still fighting the Korean War, and have recreated the Cold War with Russia. These foreign policy issues are window dressing in Trump Presidency Reality TV script. The real issue which makes the two time periods completely different, and the reason high real GDP growth is virtually impossible currently, is US foreign trade policy. In the 1950s as interest rates lifted off the zero bound, the US ran trade surpluses as Europe and Japan were re-built after WWII. However, once the trading arrangements began to reverse in the late 1960s, and the oil producing export nations decided they needed to maintain their relative standard of living to the US economy which was being juiced by high US fiscal spending growth rates, interest raced higher along with oil market driven inflation.
What finally broke the higher inflation / interest rate cycle of the 1970s? First it was shift to a “borrow and spend” policy in Washington based on cutting individual tax rates rather than a “tax and spend” policy approach. This change began to arrest inflation and bring interest rates down some in the 1980s primarily because fiscal spending growth rates began to decline. However, the real shift in US policy which affected US interest rates happened post 1989, after the fall of the Berlin Wall. It took a couple of years, and a change in Presidents from Bush I to Clinton, wherein two major changes in Washington began in the early 1990s that have driven policies in Washington DC for the past 25 years – until the election of President Trump. And those policies can be summarized as a willingness of the US government to accept a “reverse mortgage” of its own economy by running perpetual current account deficits and a corresponding policy to constrain the growth rate in fiscal spending growth in Washington DC to keep the reverse mortgage from ballooning out of control.
As a starting point to prove the relationship between the US trade deficit and the US public debt, take a look at the relationship between these two accounts over the past 25 years, compared to the time frame leading up to 1992:
At the beginning of the time period in which US trade policy dramatically shifted, China was the major instigator of the foreign trade model change as they elected to devalue their currency against the US Dollar by 30%, and have since perpetually pegged their currency against the USD at the lower value by using extensive capital controls to keep the currency from strengthen. The China economy is a model (all kinds of crazy) for storing and hoarding capital for the purpose of maintaining the weak Yuan peg against the US Dollar. Why else would the country actually build an entire 100 acre replica of the US Pentagon as shopping mall, but leave it empty with no tenants?…
Or, build a replica of Manhattan Island near the port city of Tianjin, where again, no one lives there?…
It is called capital control in an imperialist communist society.
In December of 1993 NAFTA was also signed as a treaty which opened the door for similar trade practices to evolve in Mexico where it now takes 20 Mexican Pesos to buy 1 USD; in 1990 it only took 3. And, along the way, the Mexican Central Bank expanded its balance sheet by a factor of 40 times! It is the capital control process of countries like China and Mexico, along with Japan, which has persistently applied downward pressure on US interest rates from the mid-1990s until the epic low point reached in the summer of 2016. As the data show, financing the current account deficit for the US through public financing (borrow and spend policies in Washington) has not been an issue up until the beginning of 2018, just after the Trump economic plan was passed in December. In the words of BOJ Governor Kuroda, “no debt crisis is erupting” [yet], because public financing debt sustainability has been maintained for the past 25 years. At least this is his party line for now.
Dirty Float Inversely Correlated with US Treasury 10 year Rates Just think for a moment about the paradox that has transpired as this epic interest rate downtrend cycle over the past 25 years has transpired. Countries which arguably are not as wealthy as the US, have devalued their own currency by printing their money and having their central bank hold the IOUs. The Japan BOJ currently holds over 45% of the balance of its outstanding debt, which it has purposefully used not to invest in public projects or social programs within Japan, but rather to buy assets in international markets, primarily US markets. This process is purposefully aimed at keeping their currency low relative to the US Dollar in order to maintain their share of US trade and keep vital industrial technology production capabilities within the boundaries of their own country. Essentially their perspective is – “we would rather own the apple orchard rather than just eat the apples.”
Meanwhile, the US becomes more and more indebted to these countries on paper, even though the country doing the devaluations, like Japan, have leveraged balance sheets containing assets denominated in dollars that will blow up if U.S. rates and the stock market suddenly reverse trend. And if you don’t believe the dirty float process is real, here is the macro trend data which shows the steep trend up in foreign financing of the US public finance need (i.e. budget deficit) beginning in the 1990s and continuing until recent years.
The large spike upward in 2008-2010 is particularly troublesome to me because it is almost entirely a result of China electing (most likely at the behest of the US government) to print Yuan, convert it to US Dollars and finance the $1.2 Trillion fiscal spending plan in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.
Remember, China’s sudden willingness to buy US debt was on the heels, as the prior chart shows, of large downward spikes in sources of International capital in the 2006 through 2008 timeframe to fund the US public debt need. You can see a similar large downward spike in the year 2000 time frame. In both cases when the International Bankers withdrew support for US public financing need growth (in other words, they did not even need to sell Treasuries, they just had to stop adding to their portfolio), eventually the stock market took a serious hit in valuation.
In the case of the year 2000 and 2008, the trend line upward in public financing support from international sources was not broken. In review it appears that the International Banks got what they wanted out of Washington and resumed their trade practices with the permission of Washington after the stock market tanked. You can bet that these Bankers will continue to use this ”kamikaze” method of negotiation with Donald Trump in the near future, seeing how it has been so successful in the past. The trendline is decidedly downward at the present time. In fact, the international bankers can currently sell longer term US Treasuries like the 10 Year and still see the US Dollar strengthen, thanks in large part to the continued push of bids into alternative asset markets. This is a market anomaly that can only be maintained through concerted capital controls aimed at keeping US stocks propped up while Treasury rates move higher.
International Bankers Losing Control of US Debt Sustainability under Trump's Plan What the International Banks need / want most, because they own a lot of US government paper and stocks, is US “debt sustainability” which is code for US government fiscal spending constraints and low public float of available Treasury securities. And although the US was in the process of potentially breaking the implied trade / public finance arrangement in the early years of the Obama administration, thanks to the budget “sequester” after the 2010 mid-term elections, US fiscal spending growth from 2012 through the end of the Obama administration was very low by historical standards. In addition, the Fed QE program withdrew almost $4T in public financing debt from the US market in the 2010-2014 time periods through its quantitative easing program. The result of these policies has been a trend downward in foreign purchases of US Treasury debt since 2012, and lower and lower Treasury interest rates – until Trump.
As a result of the Fed QE program and low government fiscal spending growth, foreign "dirty float" capital over the past 8 years has been chased out of the US Treasury complex, and instead channeled vigorously in recent years into US stocks, particularly in markets like the DOW ( DIA ) and S&P500 ( SPY ) which have a very high level of trading liquidity through Wall Street ETF products. And one of the reasons that the brilliant international bankers have been increasingly willing to park their dirty float “sovereign wealth fund” assets in the US stock market for the past 25 years is because they felt in control of where Washington DC was head with respect to the “sustainability of the public finance” in the words of BOJ Governor Kuroda. However, as this chart shows, the fiscal sustainability of the US financial situation is now in the process of changing dramatically from the “free for all” US trade policies that began earnest in the 1990s. In my estimation, the US public finance growth rate trend line within the next year will move well above 5% annually, and likely resemble the late 1970s early 1980s time period within a few years unless there is a change in Washington.
Trump US Public Financing and Trade Policy Building to an International Financial Showdown In my estimation, the biggest relative problem with stock and bond valuations today is that what has happened over the last 25 years is a make believe world which is only sustainable through the collusion of financial policies between International Banks (primarily the BOJ, PBoC and the ECB), and a willingness of the US government to severely constrain its growth in fiscal spending (to pay off the reverse mortgage of its GDP in order to consume more) and thereby keep the amount of debt needed by the US Treasury at a level acceptable to the international community. However, break away from this model, as President Trump policies are clearly in the process of doing, and the worldwide financial system repercussions are predictably going to be painful to some parties in the investment world, particularly central bankers and sovereign wealth funds that hold a lot of US stocks and bond assets on their balance sheets.
Currently the holders of long duration Treasury debt are beginning to feel the pain, and I see the pain creeping into lower rated long duration debt. But the pain in the credit market, other than Treasuries, is still muted. Because both the ECB and BOJ are continuing to push liquidity into the market in areas other than US Treasuries, the US Treasury rate market rather than other risk assets appears to be taking the brunt of the market adjustment force at the moment. I believe this is the shot across the bow moment for the financial markets.
The current faster increase in US Treasury rates relative to other risk assets is a clear signal to me that the big players in the world financial market, primarily sovereign governments and wealth funds heavily exposed to dollar based assets, are making significant portfolio moves in anticipation of future market pressure. The US Treasury since early April has gotten a temporary reprieve from its need to push new public borrowing needs on the market; however, it is still re-financing the maturing Treasury debt on the Fed balance sheet, which happens at known pre-scheduled times with the bulk of the maturities on the 15 th and the end of each month going forward. The 15 th of May was a noted down day in the stock market, as Treasury rates continued to move higher. A similar pattern has been in place dating back to January 31 st .
The paradox of riskier assets valued in US dollars holding or even increasing in value while lower risk Treasury assets are losing value at a faster pace is unsustainable. The longer the market dichotomy continues, the greater the risk of a Kamikaze crash landing of the BOJ, PBoC and ECB debt driven asset buying machines right into the middle of the US stock market, with the most visible targets being long FAANG ( FB ) ( AAPL ) ( AMZN ) ( NFLX ) ( GOOGL ) holders. In the aftermath of what appears to be an almost certain outcome in the near future in which the International Banks withdrawal (or just slow down) from asset buying programs precipitates a crash in the US equity market, the only question will be will the International Bankers get their way in negotiating a continuation of the past 25 year US trade policy, or will the world financial system truly embark on a different path forward? The stock market has shown volatility, but still appears to be pricing in a status quo trade model for the future. I think a less than desirable outcome for US Main Street is what the International Bankers are counting on. What I believe the market still has not come to terms with is the unsustainability of the current International Bank asset buying policies and the fact that the international trade model is broken and must change.
Daniel Moore is the author of the book Theory of Financial Relativity: Unlocking Market Mysteries that will Make You a Better Investor . All opinions and analyses shared in this article are expressly his own, and intended for information purposes only and not advice to buy or sell.
